title: A Guide to GE’s Auxiliary I/O Boards for LCI Drive Systems
author: edean
contentHtml:
Introduction

In turbine-based power generation, reliable performance starts with a precise and coordinated control system. Whether it’s a gas or steam turbine, the startup process is heavily dependent on accurate communication between sensors, controllers, and drives. A key enabler of this communication within GE’s Load Commutated Inverter (LCI) drive systems is the Auxiliary I/O Terminal Board.

These boards may not always be front and center in system diagrams, but their role is critical. This guide explores what auxiliary I/O boards do, how they integrate with GE’s LCI systems, and why they’re vital in turbine control environments.

Understanding LCI Drive Systems in Turbine Applications

GE’s LCI drives are widely used to start large synchronous motors, particularly in power plants where turbines are the core machinery. During startup, the LCI system acts as a variable frequency power source, bringing the motor (and thus the turbine shaft) up to operational speed.

This process involves a carefully coordinated sequence of control actions, monitored and adjusted in real time. To ensure smooth communication between control units and field devices, a dependable input/output interface is needed — this is where auxiliary I/O boards come into play.

What Is an Auxiliary I/O Terminal Board?

An Auxiliary I/O Terminal Board is a signal interface module that connects external field signals to the control system. It primarily handles digital inputs and outputs (I/O) such as:

  • Start/stop commands 
  • Safety interlock signals 
  • Alarm triggers 
  • Relay actuation for external devices 

The board provides terminal blocks for wiring, LED indicators for quick diagnostics, and often includes electrical isolation to protect control electronics from power surges or faults in the field wiring.

Key Functions in GE’s Control Architecture

In GE’s turbine control systems, especially those based on the Mark V and Mark VI platforms, auxiliary I/O boards are used to:

  • Receive external signals from pressure switches, temperature sensors, or safety relays 
  • Provide annunciators, actuators, or other external devices with control signals. 
  • Support logical control sequences during turbine startup and shutdown 
  • Enable diagnostics and monitoring through visual status indicators or feedback loops 

These boards are installed inside control cabinets and are connected to Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs), centralized processors, or programmable logic controllers (PLCs). In effect, they act as the hands and ears of the control system, bridging the digital world of logic with the physical world of electrical hardware.

Application in Turbine Start Systems

One of the most common uses of auxiliary I/O boards in the turbine industry is within starter systems for large synchronous motors. These motors are used to bring turbines from a standstill to synchronous speed before switching over to combustion or steam power.

Here, the I/O board plays a pivotal role by:

  • Interfacing with limit switches, auxiliary contacts, and breaker status indicators 
  • Managing safety interlocks to prevent unsafe startup conditions 
  • Triggering alarms in the event of overspeed, high temperature, or other fault conditions 
  • Executing sequences through digital output signals to contactors and relays 

This configuration guarantees both personnel and equipment protection in addition to effective turbine startup.

Maintenance and Integration Tips

Auxiliary I/O boards are generally modular and replaceable, which makes maintenance straightforward. However, it’s important to ensure that the board matches system specifications — such as voltage levels, signal types, and configuration settings.

When integrating into an existing system, careful attention must be paid to wiring practices, grounding, and isolation to avoid signal interference or hardware damage.

Conclusion

Auxiliary I/O boards may operate behind the scenes, but their impact on turbine system performance is anything but minor. In GE’s LCI drive systems, these boards serve as a crucial interface between intelligent control logic and real-world hardware.

Their role in managing signals, ensuring safety, and facilitating efficient turbine startup makes them indispensable in modern power generation environments. Understanding their function and maintenance can help engineers and operators improve reliability, minimize downtime, and optimize control strategies across the board.
